name: LearnPack Pedagogical Rubric
scope: For a subject-matter expert judging a deployed LearnPack course by taking it as a learner would, end to end. Twelve statements; each answered as agreement on the same five points. What it produces is the reference automated assessors are compared against — not a published verdict on a course, and not a score anyone reports.
evaluatorMaterials: the deployed course, all lessons, taken as a learner would take it

items.prompt: Each learning objective names something you could watch a learner do.
items.guidance: Agree if every objective names an action you could watch someone perform — solve, classify, build, debug. Disagree if objectives only list topics the course will cover, or name things that happen only in the learner's head, such as 'understand', 'learn about' or 'get familiar with'.

items.prompt: The course starts at a level its intended learners can actually begin from.
items.guidance: Agree if what the course assumes learners already know is either stated up front or fair to expect of that audience. Disagree if it requires knowledge that audience would not have, or uses ideas it never names and that audience would not bring.

items.prompt: Every learning objective is actually taught somewhere in the course.
items.guidance: Agree if every objective has a lesson, or part of a lesson, that actually teaches it — not just a mention. Disagree if any objective is only named in passing, with nothing that actually teaches it.

items.prompt: Every learning objective is checked by at least one task that shows whether the learner can actually do it.
items.guidance: Agree if every objective has a quiz, exercise, or project that would show whether a learner can actually do it. Disagree if there are no such tasks, if they check something other than the objectives, or if they only ask the learner to repeat what was said.

items.prompt: When the course teaches something new, it starts from a real problem or task, not from definitions and theory.
items.guidance: Agree if a new topic almost always opens with a concrete, real problem or task that gives a reason to learn it. Disagree if lessons start with definitions and theory, and the reason to care — if it comes at all — arrives afterwards.

items.prompt: The course shows a full example of each new skill before asking the learner to practice it.
items.guidance: Agree if every skill the course teaches is shown done, step by step, with a concrete example, before the learner practices it. Disagree if the course describes how something is done without ever showing it done, or jumps straight from description to practice.

items.prompt: Lessons connect what they teach to what the learner already knows.
items.guidance: Agree if what a lesson teaches is tied to something the learner already knows, or to everyday experience this audience would have. Disagree if what a lesson teaches arrives with no link to anything the learner brings — as a standalone chunk of information.

items.prompt: Lessons follow an order where each one builds on the ones before.
items.guidance: Agree if the lesson order is doing real work — each lesson builds on, or needs, the ones before it. Disagree if the lessons could be shuffled with little loss, because each stands on its own.

items.prompt: Later lessons use earlier ideas to build something new, instead of just repeating them on their own.
items.guidance: Agree if later lessons draw on earlier ideas to build something new, not just recap them. Disagree if earlier ideas show up again only as a restatement, disconnected from what is around them, with nothing new built from them.

items.prompt: The course says how its lessons and ideas connect, instead of leaving the learner to figure it out.
items.guidance: This is not about whether the sequence is coherent, but about whether the course says so. Agree if the course tells the learner how its parts relate: why this comes after that, what an idea builds on. Disagree if lessons are presented one after another and the learner has to work out for themselves how they relate.

items.prompt: Ideas the course builds on are introduced before they are needed.
items.guidance: Agree if every idea a lesson depends on was introduced earlier in the course, or is genuinely part of what this audience would already know. Disagree if lessons depend on ideas that were never introduced and that this audience would not be expected to bring.

items.prompt: The course asks more of the learner over time, in steps someone who has kept up could still follow.
items.guidance: Agree if the course gets steadily more demanding and each step is reachable from the one before. Disagree if it stays flat throughout, or if at least one lesson jumps far ahead of the rest of the course.

frameworks.citation: Merrill, M. D. (2002). First Principles of Instruction. ETR&D, 50(3), 43-59.
Biggs, J. (1996). Enhancing teaching through constructive alignment. Higher Education, 32, 347-364.
Anderson & Krathwohl (2001); Krathwohl (2002), Theory Into Practice, 41(4), 212-218.
Biggs & Collis (1982). Evaluating the Quality of Learning: The SOLO Taxonomy.
Schmidt, Wang & McKnight (2005); Schmidt, Houang & Cogan (2002). Curriculum coherence.
Duschl, Maeng & Sezen (2011). Learning progressions and teaching sequences.
